messages:
nate: FYI ran into a weird edge with our corporate MSI of redwoodctl + local testing. IT pushed the MSI with system account and now I have two profiles floating around (one in my user %APPDATA% and one under the system profile). When I run localserve elevated it picks the system profile and hits prod creds.

greg: ouch. can you show the paths where profiles.json ended up?

nate: sure, trimmed output:
```powershell
PS C:\> Get-ChildItem -Path $env:APPDATA\AppData\Local\Redwood -Recurse -File
C:\Users
ate\AppData\Local\Redwood\profiles.json
C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\Redwood\profiles.json
```
When the service team runs `redwoodctl localserve` from a scheduled task (runs as SYSTEM) it silently uses the systemprofile file. My dev shell (not elevated) uses my user file. Super confusing.

suzie: that explains the prod leak. MSI migration probably ran as SYSTEM during install and wrote a default profile in systemprofile. We should not treat systemprofile as a normal user config.

greg: thanks for repro. Short-term workaround: explicitly pass `--profile` and set `REDWOOD_CONFIG_DIR` to a user path, or run non-elevated. Example:
```powershell
$env:REDWOOD_CONFIG_DIR = "$env:USERPROFILE\AppData\Local\Redwood"
redwoodctl localserve --profile staging --port 8080
```
This forces the process to use the user-scoped config.

nate: that worked for me. But CI/scheduled tasks need an unattended pattern. We tried `redwoodctl login --device-code` in a startup script as SYSTEM and it writes systemprofile creds which we then can't easily share. Also the device-code flow pops a browser on the system account (no UI) and times out.

suzie: we need two fixes: 1) detect when running as an undesirable account (SYSTEM) and warn/exit unless explicitly forced, 2) add a `--scope` flag to migration/login to choose where to write (user/system/global) and an explicit `--noninteractive-exit` for device-code in automation.

greg: agreed. Also the CLI should refuse to migrate local user profiles into systemprofile without an explicit confirmation flag during MSI postinstall; silent migration is dangerous. We should also ensure the installer marks migrated profiles as migrated (atomic marker) to avoid dupes.

nate: filed a short repro gist and included commands. One additional oddity: when both profiles exist with the same profile name, redwoodctl merges them but picks fields from whichever file it reads first, causing inconsistent "expires_at" values and occasional 401s. Not guaranteed but flaky.

suzie: that sounds similar to multi-writer races others have reported. We should reconcile by prefering freshest token (expires_at/issued_at) on load and warn on conflicting ids. Also add `redwoodctl profile inspect --path` to show which file a profile came from.

greg: I'll open a PR to implement: - detect system account and print a clear hint w/ env override - add `--scope` to login/migrate - prefer freshest token when merging - add `profile inspect` command - ensure migration uses atomic temp+rename and writes marker file.

devex-bot: Created issue #1250: "installer(msi): avoid writing user profiles into systemprofile; add login/migrate --scope and CI-friendly --exit-on-complete for device auth; profile inspect and fresh-token merge"  https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwoodctl/issues/1250

it-support: adding IT note: when deploying via SCCM we should run post-install hooks as the user when possible (per-machine installs are fine but avoid migrating interactive user config into SYSTEM). I'll include the recommended `--scope user` flag once the PR lands.

nate: thanks all. For anyone blocked now: unset elevation, set REDWOOD_CONFIG_DIR to user path, and re-run login. That unblocked my local testing. Closing this thread. :white_check_mark:
